visuals.heading: Work Actually Looks Like in Each Field

items.text: Bank jobs mean fixed hours and transfers; IT jobs mean flexible or remote work with unpredictable crunch periods.
The 2025 IT layoffs were not just an entry-level story.

blocks.heading: There Is No Universal Winner, and Most

items.text: A bank job wins on protection: once you clear the exam and confirm after probation, your income survives a bad company quarter, a lost client, or an AI-driven headcount cut, because none of those things can remove a confirmed PSU employee the way they can a private-sector one.

An IT job wins on ceiling and speed: no single high-stakes exam steps your entry, pay can grow much faster in strong years, and the top of the field pays multiples of what banking ever will, for the engineers who keep their skills current enough to stay there.

blocks.heading: Questions Before You Commit to Either Path

items.text: A salary table cannot tell you which field fits your actual risk tolerance and life situation.
Banking rewards people who find genuine satisfaction in process, accuracy, and steady routine, largely the same core tasks day after day, occasionally interrupted by targets and audits.
If a structure that repeats mostly the same way daily feels calming rather than boring to you, that is a genuine signal toward banking, not a lack of ambition.

blocks.heading: Roles That Sit Between Both Worlds

items.text: Framing this as a strict either/or misses how the Indian banking and tech markets actually overlap.
Every major bank runs a large internal technology function, core banking systems, mobile and net banking apps, fraud detection, and cybersecurity.
India's FinTech and digital-lending sector hires engineers, data analysts, and product managers who understand both banking regulation and software delivery.
